## Experimental design

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/03-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

One row is a possible test trial for an infant, including rows completed by the release's exclusion code when no trial metadata or included looking time is available.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The ManyBabies Consortium's infant-directed-speech study coordinated a shared preference experiment across laboratories. This unit uses the frozen trial table from the MIT-licensed official analysis repository. One row is a possible test trial for an infant, including rows completed by the release's exclusion code when no trial metadata or included looking time is available.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809

## Experimental design

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/04-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

The trial row, assignment unit, sampling unit, laboratory, and stimulus are distinct empirical objects.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Register varies within infant: the protocol presents infant-directed speech (IDS) and adult-directed speech (ADS) trials to the same infant. Trial order varies between infants. Infants are recruited within laboratories, and paired stimuli recur across infants. Thus the trial row, assignment unit, sampling unit, laboratory, and stimulus are distinct empirical objects.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
:::

## Experimental design {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/05-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

In this study, the within-infant IDS-minus-ADS contrast is available only for infants with included looking times in both registers; a laboratory or age association is observational because neither was assigned.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The design determines which estimands are identified by the observed comparisons. A fitted model cannot recover a comparison that the design never made available. In this study, the within-infant IDS-minus-ADS contrast is available only for infants with included looking times in both registers; a laboratory or age association is observational because neither was assigned.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
:::

## The design sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/06-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

The assignment-mechanism page then compares the released order labels with a reproducible constrained allocation and distinguishes verification of a procedure from evidence that the historical implementation followed it.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Units of assignment separates possible trials, infants, laboratories, and recurring stimuli. ## The design sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/07-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

Between-participant designs use the observed second-session grouping to show what a between-group comparison estimates when the grouping variable was not randomly assigned.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Within-participant designs construct the IDS-minus-ADS contrast from infants represented in both registers. Between-participant designs use the observed second-session grouping to show what a between-group comparison estimates when the grouping variable was not randomly assigned.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
:::

## The design sequence

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/08-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

Finally, power by simulation generates new trials from an empirically fitted hierarchical model and repeats the complete planned analysis.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Counterbalancing audits the realized order and stimulus allocations rather than displaying an invented Latin square. Exclusion rules distinguish recorded metadata, included outcomes, and completed measurement opportunities. Finally, power by simulation generates new trials from an empirically fitted hierarchical model and repeats the complete planned analysis.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
:::

## Keep the claim aligned with the design

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/09-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

Likewise, method, laboratory, age, and community differences may describe this release without becoming randomized treatment effects.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Looking time is a behavioral measure. An IDS--ADS difference may support a claim about preference under the tested stimuli and procedures, but it does not uniquely identify a perceptual or social mechanism. Likewise, method, laboratory, age, and community differences may describe this release without becoming randomized treatment effects.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
:::

## Keep the claim aligned with the design

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/index/10-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/index.qmd; note-sha256: 617b4306511cbbaacc29eba331b53bb6e69a5ae2109d25147d811014fea3cc15; role: concept -->

The module thus keeps four questions visible.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The module thus keeps four questions visible: (i) which unit could independently receive a condition, (ii) which measurements repeat within that unit, (iii) which allocation or exclusion rule produced the analyzed rows, and (iv) which population or future design the contrast is meant to represent.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
:::

## Units of assignment

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/units-of-assignment/02-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/units-of-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 42f2458823dae9e4cbb5670e8053c5ec9a4d3a3a60f9477ad05d901ffc16e560; role: concept -->

We begin with that table rather than with a small constructed design.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The ManyBabies Consortium tested infants' preference for infant-directed speech (IDS) over adult-directed speech (ADS) in a shared multi-laboratory experiment. The primary report describes the stimuli, protocol, exclusions, and analyses (The ManyBabies Consortium 2020); the frozen course table comes from the official analysis repository at commit `dc3eb5b`. We begin with that table rather than with a small constructed design.

[Sources]

## Units of assignment

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/units-of-assignment/03-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/units-of-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 42f2458823dae9e4cbb5670e8053c5ec9a4d3a3a60f9477ad05d901ffc16e560; role: concept -->

No missing looking time has been imputed.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Each infant could encounter sixteen 18-second test stimuli: eight IDS stimuli and eight ADS stimuli. The official exclusion code then completed every retained infant's record to sixteen possible test-trial rows. A row may thus contain an included looking time, recorded trial metadata without an included looking time, or a completed measurement opportunity without recorded trial metadata. No missing looking time has been imputed.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

## Assignment and measurement are different maps {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/units-of-assignment/04-math; notes-page: experimental-design/units-of-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 42f2458823dae9e4cbb5670e8053c5ec9a4d3a3a60f9477ad05d901ffc16e560; role: math -->

If $Z_i$ is infant $i$'s assigned trial order, then

$$
Z_r=Z_{g(r)}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **unit of assignment**, also called the experimental unit, is the smallest entity that can independently receive a condition under the actual procedure. Let $r$ index possible trial rows and let $g(r)$ map row $r$ to its infant. If $Z_i$ is infant $i$'s assigned trial order, then

$$
Z_r=Z_{g(r)}.
$$

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

## Assignment and measurement are different maps

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/units-of-assignment/05-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/units-of-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 42f2458823dae9e4cbb5670e8053c5ec9a4d3a3a60f9477ad05d901ffc16e560; role: concept -->

The rows do not represent sixteen independent assignments.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

All sixteen possible rows from one infant share one order assignment. The rows do not represent sixteen independent assignments.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6

:::

## Assignment and measurement are different maps (1 of 2) {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/units-of-assignment/06-list; notes-page: experimental-design/units-of-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 42f2458823dae9e4cbb5670e8053c5ec9a4d3a3a60f9477ad05d901ffc16e560; role: list -->

These maps keep five roles apart:

1. A possible trial row is a measurement opportunity;
2. An infant is the sampling unit and the order-assignment unit;
3. A laboratory is a cluster within which infants were recruited and tested;
4. A paired stimulus recurs across infants;

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Other maps are needed as well. Let $l(r)$ identify the laboratory, $p(r)$ the paired stimulus when its metadata were recorded, and $R_r$ indicate whether an included looking time is present. The recorded outcome is then available only when $R_r=1$. These maps keep five roles apart: a possible trial row is a measurement opportunity. an infant is the sampling unit and the order-assignment unit. a laboratory is a cluster within which infants were recruited and tested. a paired stimulus recurs across infants.

[Sources]

https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245919900809
https://github.com/manybabies/mb1-analysis-public/tree/dc3eb5b3578057096d337203635c0759d2fc04b6
https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

These maps keep five roles apart:

5. A nonmissing looking time is an observed outcome.

::: {.notes}

Other maps are needed as well. Let $l(r)$ identify the laboratory, $p(r)$ the paired stimulus when its metadata were recorded, and $R_r$ indicate whether an included looking time is present. ## Unequal information within laboratories

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/units-of-assignment/12-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/units-of-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 42f2458823dae9e4cbb5670e8053c5ec9a4d3a3a60f9477ad05d901ffc16e560; role: concept -->

Likewise, eight recurring paired stimuli supply repeated material measurements, not eight additional infant assignments.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Additional trials may improve the measurement of a particular infant's looking behavior, and additional infants may improve the comparison across infants. They are not interchangeable. Likewise, eight recurring paired stimuli supply repeated material measurements, not eight additional infant assignments.

## Random assignment

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/random-assignment/02-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/random-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 203359bcdf557a14211249cdc43fe0a89f5d9c8ac0622aabd72090ceb82cc052; role: concept -->

It does not document the local algorithm by which every laboratory mapped a particular infant to one of those orders.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We continue with the ManyBabies 1 release introduced on the preceding page. Its design makes a useful distinction between a documented sequence and a documented allocation device. The paper reports four pseudorandom trial sequences, each containing four blocks with two IDS and two ADS trials. The release records the order attached to an infant. It does not document the local algorithm by which every laboratory mapped a particular infant to one of those orders.

[Sources]

https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

## Random assignment

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/random-assignment/03-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/random-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 203359bcdf557a14211249cdc43fe0a89f5d9c8ac0622aabd72090ceb82cc052; role: concept -->

We cannot use those labels alone to infer the probability rule used locally.

[Transcript]

## The assignment mechanism is a probability rule {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/random-assignment/04-math; notes-page: experimental-design/random-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 203359bcdf557a14211249cdc43fe0a89f5d9c8ac0622aabd72090ceb82cc052; role: math -->

Under a verified randomized allocation within laboratory, the assignment-identification link would be

$$
Z_i \mathrel{\perp} \{Y_i(1),\ldots,Y_i(4)\}\mid l(i),
$$

where $l(i)$ is the infant's laboratory.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The **assignment mechanism** specifies the probability with which each assignment unit receives each condition. Let $Z_i$ denote infant $i$'s order, and let $Y_i(z)$ denote an outcome the infant would supply under order $z$. Under a verified randomized allocation within laboratory, the assignment-identification link would be

$$
Z_i \mathrel{\perp} \{Y_i(1),\ldots,Y_i(4)\}\mid l(i),
$$

where $l(i)$ is the infant's laboratory.

[Sources]

https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

The design record must also specify how order labels were generated, concealed, and assigned.

::: {.notes}

## A relabeling diagnostic {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/random-assignment/08-math; notes-page: experimental-design/random-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 203359bcdf557a14211249cdc43fe0a89f5d9c8ac0622aabd72090ceb82cc052; role: math -->

Our statistic is the range of the four resulting order means,

$$
T(Z)=\max_z \overline{A}^{,c}_z-\min_z \overline{A}^{,c}_z,
$$

where $A_i^c=A_i-\overline A_{l(i)}$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

We can still ask whether a measured pre-outcome characteristic is unusually imbalanced relative to a transparent reference operation. Infant age varies sharply by laboratory, so comparing raw order means would mix order balance with the laboratories that contributed each order. We first center age within laboratory. Our statistic is the range of the four resulting order means,

$$
T(Z)=\max_z \overline{A}^{,c}_z-\min_z \overline{A}^{,c}_z,
$$

where $A_i^c=A_i-\overline A_{l(i)}$.

[Sources]

https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics-2e/pages/1-4-experimental-design-and-ethics
:::

We then relabel orders within each laboratory while preserving that laboratory's realized order counts.

::: {.notes}

## Assignment is not sampling

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/random-assignment/12-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/random-assignment.qmd; note-sha256: 203359bcdf557a14211249cdc43fe0a89f5d9c8ac0622aabd72090ceb82cc052; role: concept -->

Random allocation does not make laboratories or English stimuli probability samples of their respective populations.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Assignment governs how conditions are distributed among enrolled units. Sampling governs how infants, laboratories, and stimuli enter the study. Random allocation does not make laboratories or English stimuli probability samples of their respective populations.

## Within-participant designs

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/02-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: concept -->

Looking time is the measured behavior: it may index attention to the two kinds of speech, but it is not a direct measure of a particular linguistic representation.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

In the ManyBabies 1 design, speech register varies within infant. Each infant could hear both infant-directed speech (IDS) and adult-directed speech (ADS), and each register was represented by eight stimuli. Looking time is the measured behavior: it may index attention to the two kinds of speech, but it is not a direct measure of a particular linguistic representation.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Within-participant designs

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/03-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: concept -->

The participant can thus supply the condition comparison before comparisons are averaged across participants.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

In a **within-participant design**, each participant contributes observations to more than one condition. The participant can thus supply the condition comparison before comparisons are averaged across participants.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Each infant supplies a register contrast {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/04-math; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: math -->

Let $Y_{ir}$ be infant $i$'s mean included looking time in register $r$. The infant-level difference is

$$
D_i=Y_{i,\mathrm{IDS}}-Y_{i,\mathrm{ADS}},
$$

and the infant-weighted mean difference among infants observed in both registers is

$$
\overline D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $Y_{ir}$ be infant $i$'s mean included looking time in register $r$. The infant-level difference is

$$
D_i=Y_{i,\mathrm{IDS}}-Y_{i,\mathrm{ADS}},
$$

and the infant-weighted mean difference among infants observed in both registers is

$$
\overline D=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}D_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Each infant supplies a register contrast {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/05-math; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: math -->

The unit entering the final average is the infant, not the trial. If an infant-specific tendency $a_i$ adds the same amount in both registers, it cancels within that infant:

$$
(\mu_{\mathrm{IDS}}+a_i)-(\mu_{\mathrm{ADS}}+a_i)
=\mu_{\mathrm{IDS}}-\mu_{\mathrm{ADS}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The unit entering the final average is the infant, not the trial. If an infant-specific tendency $a_i$ adds the same amount in both registers, it cancels within that infant:

$$
(\mu_{\mathrm{IDS}}+a_i)-(\mu_{\mathrm{ADS}}+a_i)
=\mu_{\mathrm{IDS}}-\mu_{\mathrm{ADS}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

This cancellation does not remove stimulus variation, condition-specific infant responses, trial order, or laboratory differences.

## Unequal trial counts remain part of the target

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/12-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: concept -->

Neither target is automatically preferable; the unit used in the average must match the question.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The unweighted mean of $D_i$ gives each complete infant one contribution, even when their register means rest on different numbers of trials. A row-weighted register difference would instead give more influence to infants with more included trials. Neither target is automatically preferable; the unit used in the average must match the question.

## Unequal trial counts remain part of the target

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/13-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: concept -->

It should not be described as a reproduction of the published confirmatory analysis.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The teaching summary also differs from the paper's meta-analysis. The paper first paired IDS and ADS stimuli by stimulus number, computed an infant preference across complete pairs, and then formed laboratory and age-group effect sizes. Our simpler aggregate is designed to expose the within-infant unit. It should not be described as a reproduction of the published confirmatory analysis.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

## Order can modify a within-infant contrast (1 of 2) {.compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/within-participant-designs/14-list; notes-page: experimental-design/within-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: f04880be2ec6282e7eb3e8f91756315f61dd3a2c841e08775d3264d0d1e99e9a; role: list -->

This counterbalancing distributes register over position, but it does not make carryover impossible.

1. Why must the IDS and ADS means be joined by infant before subtraction?
2. Which infant-specific component cancels under the additive expression above?
3. How would trial weighting change the target of the mean difference?

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A **carryover effect** occurs when an earlier condition changes a later response. Attention may decline over the session, and earlier speech may change what an infant attends to later. ManyBabies used four pseudorandom sequences that alternated register within four-trial blocks. This counterbalancing distributes register over position, but it does not make carryover impossible. Why must the IDS and ADS means be joined by infant before subtraction? Which infant-specific component cancels under the additive expression above? How would trial weighting change the target of the mean difference?

## Between-participant designs

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/02-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: concept -->

One infant is associated with one order across all sixteen possible test-trial rows.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

ManyBabies 1 combines two condition structures. Speech register varies within infant, while the four pseudorandom trial orders vary between infants. One infant is associated with one order across all sixteen possible test-trial rows.

## Between-participant designs

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/03-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: concept -->

The factor comparison is across groups rather than within the same participant.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

In a **between-participant design**, each participant contributes observations to only one level of a factor. The factor comparison is across groups rather than within the same participant.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## A group contrast over assigned order {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/04-math; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: math -->

Let $Y_i$ be infant $i$'s mean log looking time over included trials, and let $Z_i$ identify the infant's assigned order. The mean in order group $z$ is

$$
\overline Y_z=\frac{1}{n_z}\sum_{i:Z_i=z}Y_i.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $Y_i$ be infant $i$'s mean log looking time over included trials, and let $Z_i$ identify the infant's assigned order. The mean in order group $z$ is

$$
\overline Y_z=\frac{1}{n_z}\sum_{i:Z_i=z}Y_i.
$$

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/09-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: concept -->

It is a between-infant factor, but it is not the speech-register contrast that motivated the experiment.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

This plot does not estimate a linguistic treatment effect. Trial order was used to distribute register and paired stimulus identity over session position. It is a between-infant factor, but it is not the speech-register contrast that motivated the experiment.

## Order is a nuisance assignment

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/10-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: concept -->

They should not be labeled causal effects of order.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The documented evidence about allocation also limits interpretation. Because the public source does not specify each laboratory's infant-to-order allocation device, differences among these four realized groups are descriptive. They should not be labeled causal effects of order.

## Trials improve an infant summary, not group replication

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/11-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: concept -->

They do not increase $n_z$, because order was attached once to the infant.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The release contains 26,895 included trial outcomes from 2,302 infants. More included trials may make an infant’s $Y_i$ less sensitive to a particular stimulus. They do not increase $n_z$, because order was attached once to the infant.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Trials improve an infant summary, not group replication

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/between-participant-designs/12-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/between-participant-designs.qmd; note-sha256: b5d4a32558835703a7889995a39402d54d03912a999dcd5e039e887bb38deb93; role: concept -->

This choice matches the between-infant comparison in the equation, though the figure remains descriptive.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

A trial-weighted group mean would give more influence to infants with more included trials. The displayed analysis instead gives every infant with an outcome one group-level contribution. This choice matches the between-infant comparison in the equation, though the figure remains descriptive.

## Counterbalancing

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/counterbalancing/02-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/counterbalancing.qmd; note-sha256: 4ddf5bfa6f198e8a631f6c3414ff96c66818f3e8bbdee6b4ebef67eb23043f81; role: concept -->

We can recover the realized order templates from the released trial table.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

ManyBabies 1 used four pseudorandom trial orders to distribute register and paired stimulus identity over the sixteen test positions. Each order contained four alternating blocks, each with two infant-directed-speech (IDS) and two adult-directed-speech (ADS) trials. The same IDS and ADS stimulus numbers formed pairs. We can recover the realized order templates from the released trial table.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Counterbalancing

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/counterbalancing/03-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/counterbalancing.qmd; note-sha256: 4ddf5bfa6f198e8a631f6c3414ff96c66818f3e8bbdee6b4ebef67eb23043f81; role: concept -->

In this study, the constraint makes register available within infant while distributing register and paired stimulus identity over trial position.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

**Counterbalancing** constrains how conditions and materials are distributed across orders. It does not create independent trials. In this study, the constraint makes register available within infant while distributing register and paired stimulus identity over trial position.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

## Reconstructing the order templates

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/counterbalancing/04-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/counterbalancing.qmd; note-sha256: 4ddf5bfa6f198e8a631f6c3414ff96c66818f3e8bbdee6b4ebef67eb23043f81; role: concept -->

We recover the modal register and stimulus number for each cell, then check the resulting template.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Protocol deviations mean that the released rows need not agree perfectly within every order-by-position cell. We recover the modal register and stimulus number for each cell, then check the resulting template.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/

## Reconstructing the order templates {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/counterbalancing/05-math; notes-page: experimental-design/counterbalancing.qmd; note-sha256: 4ddf5bfa6f198e8a631f6c3414ff96c66818f3e8bbdee6b4ebef67eb23043f81; role: math -->

Let $R_{ot}$ and $P_{ot}$ denote the modal register and paired stimulus at position $t$ in order $o$. The checks above establish the empirical margins

$$
\sum_t I(R_{ot}=\mathrm{IDS})
=\sum_t I(R_{ot}=\mathrm{ADS})=8,
$$

and, for every pair $p$ in every order $o$,

$$
\sum_t I(P_{ot}=p)=2,
\qquad
\sum_t I(P_{ot}=p,R_{ot}=r)=1
$$

for each register $r$.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $R_{ot}$ and $P_{ot}$ denote the modal register and paired stimulus at position $t$ in order $o$. The checks above establish the empirical margins

$$
\sum_t I(R_{ot}=\mathrm{IDS})
=\sum_t I(R_{ot}=\mathrm{ADS})=8,
$$

and, for every pair $p$ in every order $o$,

$$
\sum_t I(P_{ot}=p)=2,
\qquad
\sum_t I(P_{ot}=p,R_{ot}=r)=1
$$

for each register $r$.

[Sources]

https://opentextbc.ca/researchmethods/chapter/experimental-design/
:::

1. Which margin verifies equal IDS and ADS counts within an order?

[Transcript]

Counterbalancing separates register from a fixed position and paired stimulus in the planned sequence. It does not remove dependence: trials still repeat within infants, stimuli recur across infants, and infants remain nested within laboratories. ## Exclusion rules

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/exclusion-rules/02-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd; note-sha256: a5630b7c9ab48d8ee5c14dc8a5861ec5ba9ad20d0f5af8a7ca107630dc832947; role: concept -->

Consequently, a row without an included looking time need not represent one single event.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

The ManyBabies 1 release is the output of a sequential exclusion pipeline. The paper describes participant rules, session-level errors, trial-level errors, a minimum included looking time, and a laboratory inclusion rule. The official script then completes every retained infant to sixteen possible test-trial rows. Consequently, a row without an included looking time need not represent one single event.

[Sources]

Course note: experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd
:::

## Retention enters the estimand {.equation-slide}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/exclusion-rules/03-math; notes-page: experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd; note-sha256: a5630b7c9ab48d8ee5c14dc8a5861ec5ba9ad20d0f5af8a7ca107630dc832947; role: math -->

Let $R_r=1$ when possible trial row $r$ contains a looking time retained by the released pipeline and let $R_r=0$ otherwise. A row-weighted register contrast among retained outcomes is

$$
\Delta_{R=1}
=\mathbb{E}[Y_r\mid Z_r=\mathrm{IDS},R_r=1]
-\mathbb{E}[Y_r\mid Z_r=\mathrm{ADS},R_r=1].
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $R_r=1$ when possible trial row $r$ contains a looking time retained by the released pipeline and let $R_r=0$ otherwise. A row-weighted register contrast among retained outcomes is

$$
\Delta_{R=1}
=\mathbb{E}[Y_r\mid Z_r=\mathrm{IDS},R_r=1]
-\mathbb{E}[Y_r\mid Z_r=\mathrm{ADS},R_r=1].
$$

[Sources]

Course note: experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd

## Register and analysis-set margins

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/exclusion-rules/11-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd; note-sha256: a5630b7c9ab48d8ee5c14dc8a5861ec5ba9ad20d0f5af8a7ca107630dc832947; role: concept -->

We can examine the thresholds considered in the paper's sensitivity analysis without reversing the official pipeline.

## Reporting the flow without overreconstruction

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/exclusion-rules/16-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/exclusion-rules.qmd; note-sha256: a5630b7c9ab48d8ee5c14dc8a5861ec5ba9ad20d0f5af8a7ca107630dc832947; role: concept -->

The teaching RDS records their final consequences through `trial_missing` and preserves the completion distinction through `trial_metadata_observed`.

::: {.notes}

A reconstructible design report should distinguish (i) original participant exclusions, (ii) session- or trial-level error decisions, (iii) the minimum-looking-time rule, and (iv) rows created to represent later possible trials. Drawing independent looking times would answer a different question, no matter how many draws were used.

## Calibrating a data-generating process {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/power-by-simulation/04-math; notes-page: experimental-design/power-by-simulation.qmd; note-sha256: 9c5d0147c20ab41a36d7ea2f1434ab95a1659761b6e4f00ef59354ad4156d247; role: math -->

Power is conditional on a data-generating process. We first fit a compact model to the 26,895 included looking times:

$$
\log Y_{lsip}
=\beta_0+\beta_{\mathrm{IDS}}I_{\mathrm{IDS}}
+\beta_t(t-\overline t)+b_l+b_{i(l)}+b_p+\epsilon,
$$

where $l$ indexes laboratory, $i$ infant, $p$ paired stimulus, and $t$ trial position.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Power is conditional on a data-generating process. We first fit a compact model to the 26,895 included looking times:

$$
\log Y_{lsip}
=\beta_0+\beta_{\mathrm{IDS}}I_{\mathrm{IDS}}
+\beta_t(t-\overline t)+b_l+b_{i(l)}+b_p+\epsilon,
$$

where $l$ indexes laboratory, $i$ infant, $p$ paired stimulus, and $t$ trial position.

[Sources]

https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187
:::

## Power and Monte Carlo error {.equation-slide .compact}

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/power-by-simulation/10-math; notes-page: experimental-design/power-by-simulation.qmd; note-sha256: 9c5d0147c20ab41a36d7ea2f1434ab95a1659761b6e4f00ef59354ad4156d247; role: math -->

If $A(Y)=1$ when the two-sided Wald interval for the IDS coefficient excludes zero, then

$$
\operatorname{Power}(G)=\mathbb{P}_G\{A(Y)=1\}.
$$

With $S$ simulated studies and detection proportion $\widehat p$, the estimated Monte Carlo standard error is

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{S}}.
$$

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Let $G$ be the complete generating process and let $A(Y)$ be the decision returned by the planned analysis for simulated data $Y$. If $A(Y)=1$ when the two-sided Wald interval for the IDS coefficient excludes zero, then

$$
\operatorname{Power}(G)=\mathbb{P}_G\{A(Y)=1\}.
$$

With $S$ simulated studies and detection proportion $\widehat p$, the estimated Monte Carlo standard error is

$$
\operatorname{MCSE}
=\sqrt{\frac{\widehat p(1-\widehat p)}{S}}.
$$

[Sources]

https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187
:::

## Power and Monte Carlo error

<!-- generated-slide-id: experimental-design/power-by-simulation/11-concept; notes-page: experimental-design/power-by-simulation.qmd; note-sha256: 9c5d0147c20ab41a36d7ea2f1434ab95a1659761b6e4f00ef59354ad4156d247; role: concept -->

It does not add infants or laboratories to the planned experiment.

::: {.notes}
[Transcript]

Increasing $S$ reduces numerical uncertainty about the simulation result. It does not add infants or laboratories to the planned experiment.

[Sources]

https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=187
:::

## What the simulation supports
